title: Guru Amar Das's gurpurab
hook: remembered at Goindval, the well of eighty-four steps

segments.voice: Yesterday, Guru Angad's gurpurab, and your line: the script and the kitchen. It ends a week that closed the shabads for a life, began the month at Sangrand, looked up at the full moon, talked kindly about dates, and visited the city of the pool. Today, a well. Day six hundred eighty-six.
screen: `A HYMN FOR EVERY TURN · THE MONTH BEGINS · FULL MOON · DATES · THE POOL · THE SCRIPT AND THE KITCHEN.`

segments.voice: Most of us start new things young: a career at twenty-two, a family at thirty. So here's a life that runs the other way. A man spends six decades as a devout pilgrim of his own tradition, walking to the Ganges again and again. Then, past sixty, he hears a young woman singing Guru Nanak's hymns while she churns butter, and everything changes. Over a decade later, in his seventies, he becomes the third Guru. Today: Guru Amar Das's gurpurab.
screen: `MOST OF US START YOUNG.` → `SIXTY YEARS A PILGRIM.` → `A SONG AT THE BUTTER CHURN.`

segments.voice: Guru Amar Das was born in 1479. The young woman singing at the churn was Bibi Amro, Guru Angad's daughter, married into his family. Tradition says he was so moved that he went to Khadur, and for years served Guru Angad: carrying water from the river before dawn, every day. In 1552, at about seventy-three, he became Guru. He settled at Goindval, on the river Beas, and two things there are remembered on his gurpurab. The first is the langar. Tradition says he asked everyone who came to eat in the free kitchen first, sitting together on the floor, before meeting him: high caste and low, rich and poor, side by side. Sikhs remember a saying linked to him: first the pangat, the row of people eating, then the sangat, the gathering. The second is the baoli, a stepwell. He had a deep well built at Goindval, with steps leading down to the water: eighty-four of them. Water for a dry town, open to everyone, with no caste rule at the bottom. Today many pilgrims walk down to the water and recite the Japji Sahib on each of the eighty-four steps, a long, slow devotion. Some Sikhs connect it to the old Indian idea of eighty-four lakh lives; others simply love it as a practice of patience, and teachers note the Gurus taught that liberation comes by grace and the Name, not by counting. Either way, it's a picture of the third Guru himself: going down, step by step, slowly, toward water.
screen: `A PILGRIM, AND A SONG AT THE CHURN.` · `PANGAT FIRST, THEN SANGAT.` · `THE BAOLI AT GOINDVAL.` · `ONE JAPJI ON EACH STEP.` · then, large: `EIGHTY-FOUR STEPS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drink water slowly. Pour a glass of water and sit with it. Look at it first. Think of the people at Goindval, walking down eighty-four steps to reach it. Then drink, in small sips, slowly, noticing the cool of it, the way it goes down. Between sips, breathe. Let the glass take the whole length of the bell if it can. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each sip. The bell holds the time.
Guru Amar Das's gurpurab. The third Guru's birthday, remembered at Goindval: the langar where all sat together, and the well of eighty-four steps.
Your line: eighty-four steps. Today, take one task you've been rushing and go down into it slowly, one step at a time. Day six hundred eighty-six.
